6.1 Prohibited Discrimination. Employees must not discriminate against another employee, applicant, customer, or other individual in connection with company activities. Prohibited
discrimination includes unfair treatment based on characteristics protected by applicable law or
company policy.

6.2 Workplace Harassment. Harassment, including verbal, physical, visual, or written conduct that violates applicable law or company policy, is prohibited. Employees must not engage in
conduct that creates an intimidating, hostile, humiliating, or offensive working environment.

6.3 Sexual Harassment. Unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, sexually explicit comments, or other unwelcome sexual conduct are prohibited. Conduct may violate this policy
whether it occurs in person, through company communication systems, or during company-
related events.

6.4 Verbal and Written Conduct. Employees must not use threatening, degrading, insulting, or discriminatory language toward coworkers or other individuals in connection with their work.
This requirement applies to workplace conversations, company email, messaging systems, and
other company communication channels.

6.5 Physical Conduct. Unwanted physical contact, threats of physical harm, intimidation, or other inappropriate physical conduct are prohibited in company workplaces and during
company-sponsored activities.

6.6 Reporting to Management. Employees who experience or observe conduct that may violate this policy may report the concern to their manager or the Human Resources department.
Reports should be made as soon as reasonably possible after the employee becomes aware of
the concern.

6.7 Human Resources Reporting Channel. Employees may submit harassment or discrimination complaints directly to Human Resources without first reporting the matter to their immediate
manager. Human Resources will document the complaint and determine the appropriate review
process.

6.8 Confidential Reporting. Employees who are uncomfortable reporting a concern through management or Human Resources may use the company's designated confidential reporting
channel. Confidentiality cannot be guaranteed in every investigation because information may
need to be shared to review and address a complaint.

6.9 Investigation Process. Reported concerns will be reviewed through an appropriate investigation or fact-finding process. Employees involved in an investigation are expected to
cooperate and provide accurate information when requested.

6.10 Protection Against Retaliation. Retaliation against an employee for making a good-faith report, participating in an investigation, or raising a concern under this policy is prohibited.
Employees who believe they have experienced retaliation should report the concern through
Human Resources or the designated reporting channel.

6.11 False or Misleading Reports. Employees are expected to provide information honestly when making or participating in a complaint. Knowingly providing materially false information
during an investigation may result in disciplinary review.

6.12 Workplace Events and Remote Work. This policy applies to conduct occurring at company offices, company-sponsored events, business travel, and company communication or
collaboration systems used for work. Remote work does not exempt an employee from the
requirements of this policy.

6.13 Manager Responsibilities. Managers who receive a complaint or become aware of conduct that may violate this policy must promptly refer the matter through the designated reporting
process. Managers must not discourage an employee from reporting a concern.

6.14 Policy Compliance. Employees are responsible for following this policy and cooperating with authorized investigations. Violations may result in corrective or disciplinary action in
accordance with applicable company procedures.

5.1 Professional Workplace Behavior. Employees are expected to communicate respectfully with coworkers, managers, customers, and other individuals they interact with while performing
their duties. Employees must not engage in threatening, abusive, discriminatory, or intentionally
disruptive behavior in the workplace or during company-related activities.

5.2 Attendance and Workplace Responsibilities. Employees are expected to follow their approved work schedules and attend required meetings and workplace activities. Repeated
failure to follow an approved schedule may result in management review.

5.3 Conflicts of Interest. Employees must disclose actual or potential conflicts of interest when their personal, financial, or outside business interests could interfere with their responsibilities
to the company. Employees must notify their manager or the designated compliance contact
within 10 business days after becoming aware of a potential conflict.

5.4 Outside Employment. Employees may participate in outside employment or business activities provided that the activity does not interfere with their company responsibilities,
involve unauthorized use of company resources, or create a conflict of interest. Employees must
obtain written approval before accepting outside work that involves a current company
customer, supplier, or direct competitor.

5.5 Gifts and Business Benefits. Employees must not accept gifts, payments, discounts, or other benefits when accepting them could influence, or reasonably appear to influence, a business
decision. Gifts with a value exceeding $100 must be disclosed to the employee's manager within
5 business days.

5.6 Company Equipment. Company-issued computers, mobile devices, software, and other equipment must primarily be used for authorized business activities. Limited personal use is
permitted when it does not interfere with work responsibilities, violate company policy, create a
security risk, or result in significant additional costs.

5.7 Company Internet and Communication Resources. Company networks, email accounts, messaging systems, and internet access must not be used to conduct unauthorized commercial
activities, distribute malicious software, access prohibited material, or interfere with another
employee's ability to work.

5.8 Personal Storage and Software. Employees must not install unauthorized software on company-managed devices or transfer company information to personal cloud-storage accounts
without authorization. Software required for business purposes must be obtained through the
approved IT process.

5.9 Confidential Information. Employees must protect confidential company information and must not disclose it to unauthorized individuals. Confidential information may include customer
information, internal financial information, employee records, business plans, and non-public
operational information.

5.10 Use of Company Resources for Personal Activities. Employees may not use company equipment, facilities, accounts, funds, or other resources for personal commercial activities.
Limited personal use of company resources is permitted only when it is incidental and does not
interfere with company operations.

5.11 Reporting Misconduct. Employees who become aware of suspected misconduct, unauthorized use of company resources, or a potential conflict of interest should report the
matter through the designated reporting channel or to their manager. Reports should be made
as soon as reasonably possible after the employee becomes aware of the concern.

5.12 Policy Compliance. Employees are responsible for understanding and complying with this policy. Violations may result in review or disciplinary action in accordance with applicable
company procedures. An exception granted to one employee does not automatically apply to
another employee.

7.1 Informal Resolution. Employees are encouraged to discuss workplace concerns with their immediate manager when appropriate. Informal discussions should normally be attempted
before submitting a formal grievance unless the concern involves the manager, requires
confidentiality, or is otherwise unsuitable for informal resolution.

7.2 Formal Grievance. Employees may submit a formal grievance when a workplace concern cannot be resolved informally or when the employee believes formal review is necessary.
Formal grievances should describe the concern, relevant events, dates, individuals involved, and
any supporting information available to the employee.

7.3 Submission Deadline. A formal grievance should normally be submitted within 15 business days of the event or decision giving rise to the concern. Human Resources may accept a later
submission when there is a reasonable explanation for the delay.

7.4 Initial Management Review. When a grievance concerns a manager's decision or workplace practice, the manager or designated reviewer should acknowledge receipt within 3 business
days and determine whether additional information is required.

7.5 Human Resources Review. Employees may submit a grievance directly to Human Resources when the concern involves their immediate manager, when informal resolution is inappropriate,
or when the employee believes the initial review did not adequately address the concern.

7.6 Supporting Information. Employees may provide relevant documents, messages, records, or other information supporting their grievance. Employees should distinguish between
information they directly observed and information received from another person.

7.7 Investigation and Fact-Finding. Human Resources or another designated reviewer may interview the employee, managers, witnesses, or other relevant individuals when additional
fact-finding is necessary. Employees participating in a review are expected to provide accurate
information and cooperate with reasonable requests.

7.8 Initial Decision. Following review of a formal grievance, the designated reviewer will communicate the outcome to the employee. The outcome may include confirmation of an
existing decision, modification of a workplace practice, additional review, or another
appropriate corrective action.

7.9 Escalation. An employee who disagrees with the outcome of an initial grievance review may request escalation to the next designated review level. An escalation request should normally
be submitted within 10 business days after the employee receives the initial decision.

7.10 Second-Level Review. A second-level review may be conducted by Human Resources, a department leader, or another designated reviewer who was not responsible for the original
decision when reasonably practicable.

7.11 Final Internal Review. After completion of the second-level review, an employee may request a final internal review when the grievance involves a significant procedural concern or
material information that was not considered previously. The request should normally be
submitted within 5 business days of the second-level decision.

7.12 Confidentiality. Information relating to a grievance will be shared only with individuals who have a legitimate need to participate in reviewing or resolving the concern. Complete
confidentiality cannot be guaranteed when information is necessary to conduct an appropriate
review.

7.13 Protection Against Retaliation. Retaliation against an employee for submitting a grievance in good faith, participating in a grievance review, or providing relevant information is prohibited.
Employees who believe they have experienced retaliation should report the concern through
Human Resources or another designated reporting channel.

7.14 Anonymous Complaints. Anonymous complaints may be submitted through an available reporting channel. The organization may review an anonymous complaint when sufficient
information is provided, although the ability to investigate or provide a response may be
limited.

7.15 Records and Documentation. Records associated with formal grievances and their outcomes should be maintained by the designated department in accordance with applicable
record-retention requirements. Employees should not alter or destroy relevant records after
submitting a grievance.

7.16 Policy Compliance. Employees and managers involved in the grievance process are expected to follow the required procedures and cooperate with authorized reviews. Knowingly
providing materially false information during a grievance review may result in disciplinary
review.

10.1 Resignation Notice Period. Employees who voluntarily resign must provide written notice to their manager and Human Resources. The standard resignation notice period is 30 calendar
days unless the employee's employment agreement specifies a different period.

10.2 Probationary Notice Period. Employees who resign during their probationary period must provide 14 calendar days of written notice unless a different requirement is specified in their
employment agreement.

10.3 Notice Submission. A resignation becomes effective when the written resignation is received by the employee's manager or Human Resources. The resignation should include the
employee's intended final working date.

10.4 Notice Period Changes. A manager may approve a shorter notice period when operational circumstances permit. An employee must not assume that a shorter notice period has been
approved without written confirmation.

10.5 Handover Responsibilities. During the notice period, employees are expected to complete assigned work, document important procedures, and transfer relevant responsibilities to the
designated employee or manager.

10.6 Exit Clearance. Employees must complete the required exit-clearance process before their final working day. Clearance may include confirmation from Human Resources, IT, Finance,
Facilities, and other departments with responsibility for company property or outstanding
obligations.

10.7 Company Equipment Return. All company-issued equipment, including laptops, monitors, headsets, mobile devices, access cards, and other assigned property, must be returned in
working condition within 5 business days of the employee's last working day unless IT or
another authorized department provides different instructions.

10.8 Access Termination. Company system access should be disabled in accordance with the employee's final working date and applicable security procedures. Employees must not retain or
use company accounts after their employment has ended.

10.9 Confidential Information. Employees must return or delete company information from unauthorized personal locations and must continue to protect confidential information after
leaving the company when applicable obligations survive termination.

10.10 Outstanding Expenses. Employees must submit eligible outstanding business expenses and supporting receipts before their final working day whenever practicable. Expenses
submitted after departure may be processed according to the applicable expense procedures.

10.11 Final Settlement. Final salary, approved outstanding expenses, applicable accrued amounts, and other required settlement items should normally be processed within 15 business
days after the employee's last working day, subject to completion of required payroll and
clearance procedures.

10.12 Clearance Delays. When required company property has not been returned or required clearance information remains incomplete, processing of certain settlement items may be
delayed to the extent permitted by applicable procedures and law.

10.13 Exit Interview. Human Resources may request an exit interview before or after the employee's final working day. Employees may provide feedback regarding their work
experience, management, workplace practices, and reasons for leaving.

10.14 Employment Records. Human Resources is responsible for updating the employee's employment record and maintaining required exit documentation in accordance with applicable
record-retention requirements.

10.15 Final Confirmation. The employee's final working date, completion of required clearance, return of company property, and completion of applicable settlement procedures should be
documented by the responsible departments.

10.16 Policy Compliance. Employees and responsible departments must follow the applicable offboarding procedures and timelines. Exceptions to the standard process require approval from
the appropriate manager or Human Resources.

9.1 Pre-Employment Documentation. New employees must provide the required employment and identification documents before or on their first working day. Required documentation may
include proof of identity, employment forms, tax documentation, emergency contact
information, and other documents specified by Human Resources.

9.2 HR Registration. Human Resources must create the employee's personnel record and enter the required employment information into the designated HR system. The employee's
department, position, manager, employment start date, and work arrangement should be
recorded during the onboarding process.

9.3 First-Day Orientation. New employees must complete the initial onboarding orientation on their first working day unless an alternative schedule has been approved. The orientation covers
workplace procedures, applicable policies, organizational expectations, and basic administrative
requirements.

9.4 Employee Accounts. Required company accounts should normally be requested on or before the employee's first working day. Access should be limited to the systems and
information necessary for the employee's assigned responsibilities.

9.5 IT Equipment. New full-time employees receive standard company equipment in accordance with the IT Equipment and Support Policy. Equipment that is not part of the
standard issue package requires the applicable approval before it is provided.

9.6 Equipment Assignment. Employees receiving company equipment must acknowledge receipt through the designated IT or asset-management process. The equipment record should
include the assigned employee, equipment identification information, and assignment date.

9.7 Security Setup. New employees must complete required account-security procedures before accessing systems containing company information. This may include password setup,
multi-factor authentication, security training, and other controls required by IT.

9.8 Department Introduction. The employee's manager should introduce the employee to the relevant team members and explain the employee's primary responsibilities, reporting
structure, work schedule, and initial priorities.

9.9 Required Training. New employees must complete mandatory onboarding training within the applicable training period. Required training may include information security, workplace
conduct, confidentiality, safety, and other training relevant to the employee's role.

9.10 First-Week Completion. The employee should complete the core onboarding requirements within the first 5 business days of employment unless a specific requirement has a different
deadline.

9.11 Thirty-Day Review. The manager should conduct an initial onboarding review approximately 30 calendar days after the employee's start date. The review may be used to
identify unresolved access issues, training requirements, role clarification, or other onboarding
needs.

9.12 Missing Documentation. When required documentation is incomplete, Human Resources may request the missing information from the employee. Certain administrative or system-
access activities may remain pending until required documentation has been provided.

9.13 Remote Employee Onboarding. Employees approved to work remotely may complete onboarding activities electronically when an in-person activity is not required. Remote
onboarding does not remove the employee's obligation to complete required documentation,
training, security procedures, or equipment acknowledgment.

9.14 Onboarding Responsibilities. Human Resources is responsible for coordinating employment documentation and administrative setup. IT is responsible for approved account
and equipment setup, while the employee's manager is responsible for role-specific orientation
and initial work assignments.

9.15 Onboarding Completion. Onboarding is considered complete when the required HR documentation, system access, equipment assignment, mandatory training, and department-
specific setup have been completed or formally recorded as pending.

9.16 Policy Compliance. New employees and responsible departments must complete onboarding requirements within the applicable timelines. Exceptions to the standard
onboarding process require approval from the appropriate department or Human Resources.

11.1 Overtime Eligibility. Employees whose positions are designated as eligible for overtime may receive overtime compensation for hours worked beyond their standard scheduled hours
when the overtime has been properly authorized and recorded. Employees classified as exempt
from overtime are not eligible for overtime compensation under this policy.

11.2 Standard Working Hours. The standard full-time work schedule is 40 hours per week unless the employee's employment agreement or applicable department schedule specifies a
different arrangement. Hours worked during the employee's normal schedule do not constitute
overtime solely because they occur outside the employee's preferred working time.

11.3 Overtime Approval. Employees must obtain manager approval before working overtime whenever reasonably practicable. Employees must not intentionally work additional hours
without authorization with the expectation that the additional hours will automatically qualify
for overtime compensation.

11.4 Emergency Overtime. When an urgent operational or technical situation requires immediate work and advance approval is not reasonably possible, an eligible employee may
work the required additional hours and must notify their manager as soon as reasonably
practicable.

11.5 Overtime Rate. Approved overtime worked by eligible employees is compensated at 1.5 times the employee's regular hourly rate unless a different rate is required by an applicable
employment agreement or governing requirement.

11.6 Weekend Overtime. Approved overtime performed on a scheduled weekend is compensated at the applicable overtime rate. Weekend work does not automatically qualify for
a higher rate unless a separate compensation rule applies.

11.7 Holiday Overtime. Work performed on a designated company holiday may be subject to a separate holiday compensation rule. Employees should obtain confirmation from Human
Resources or Payroll before working on a holiday when compensation treatment is unclear.
11.8 Overtime Recording. Employees must accurately record the date, start time, end time, and total hours worked for each overtime period through the designated timekeeping system.

11.9 Weekly Overtime Threshold. For employees whose standard schedule is 40 hours per week, hours worked beyond 40 hours in the applicable workweek may qualify as overtime when
the employee is eligible and the additional work has been approved.

11.10 Manager Responsibilities. Managers are responsible for reviewing overtime requests, confirming that additional work is necessary, and ensuring that approved overtime is accurately
recorded for payroll processing.

11.11 Unapproved Overtime. Employees should not perform recurring or planned overtime without prior approval. Where an eligible employee performs additional work without obtaining
required approval, the employee must report the hours accurately and the organization will
determine the applicable treatment under its procedures.

11.12 Remote and Hybrid Employees. Employees working under a remote or hybrid arrangement are subject to the same overtime eligibility and approval requirements as
employees working from an organizational office. Working remotely does not independently
create entitlement to overtime compensation.

11.13 Overtime During Probation. Employees in their probationary period may be eligible for overtime when their position is designated as overtime-eligible and the overtime has been
properly approved and recorded.

11.14 Payroll Processing. Approved overtime hours should normally be submitted through the designated timekeeping system before the payroll cutoff for the applicable pay period. Overtime
submitted after the cutoff may be processed in the following payroll cycle.

11.15 Overtime Limits. Managers should monitor overtime to prevent excessive working hours and should obtain additional approval when an employee is expected to work more than 10
overtime hours in a single workweek.

11.16 Policy Compliance. Employees and managers are responsible for accurately recording and approving overtime. Deliberately misreporting working hours or repeatedly bypassing the
required approval process may result in disciplinary review.

12.1 Review Cycle. All regular employees are normally evaluated through a formal performance review once every 12 months. The annual review cycle is intended to assess performance
against established responsibilities, objectives, and behavioral expectations.

12.2 Mid-Year Review. Managers should conduct a mid-year performance discussion approximately 6 months after the employee's annual review. The discussion may be used to
review progress, identify development needs, and adjust objectives when business priorities
have changed.

12.3 New Employees. Employees who have not completed their probationary period may be evaluated through the probation process rather than the standard annual performance review
cycle. After confirmation, the employee is included in the applicable performance review cycle.

12.4 Performance Criteria. Performance reviews may consider quality of work, achievement of objectives, productivity, communication, teamwork, attendance, problem-solving, professional
conduct, and other responsibilities relevant to the employee's position.

12.5 Rating Scale. Employee performance is assessed using a five-level rating scale: 1 — Does Not Meet Expectations, 2 — Partially Meets Expectations, 3 — Meets Expectations, 4 —
Exceeds Expectations, and 5 — Exceptional Performance.

12.6 Rating Definitions. A rating of 3 indicates that the employee consistently meets the normal expectations of the position. Ratings of 4 or 5 indicate performance above the standard
expectations, while ratings of 1 or 2 indicate that one or more significant performance
expectations have not been consistently achieved.

12.7 Manager Assessment. The employee's manager is responsible for preparing the performance assessment using available performance information and the requirements of the
employee's position. Managers should provide specific examples supporting significant positive
or negative assessments.

12.8 Employee Discussion. Employees should have an opportunity to discuss their performance review with their manager before the review is finalized. Employees may provide comments or
additional information that they believe is relevant to the assessment.

12.9 Final Rating. The final performance rating should be documented through the designated HR process. Completion of the review discussion does not automatically require the manager to
change the proposed rating.

12.10 Performance Improvement. Employees receiving a rating below the expected performance level may be required to participate in a performance improvement process. The
process may establish specific objectives, review dates, training requirements, and expected
improvements.

12.11 Rating Appeal. An employee who believes that a final performance rating contains a material factual error or was determined without appropriate consideration of relevant
performance information may submit an appeal to Human Resources within 10 business days of
receiving the finalized review.

12.12 Appeal Documentation. A performance-rating appeal should identify the specific rating being challenged, explain the basis for the appeal, and provide relevant supporting information.
General disagreement with a manager's judgment without supporting information may not
require a change to the rating.

12.13 Appeal Review. Human Resources may review the employee's appeal, the manager's assessment, supporting documentation, and other relevant information. When appropriate, HR
may request additional information from the employee or manager.

12.14 Appeal Outcome. The appeal review may confirm the original rating, require correction of a documented factual error, or request that the review be reconsidered through the designated
process. The employee should normally receive the appeal outcome within 15 business days
after the required information has been received.

12.15 Confidentiality. Performance reviews and associated records should be handled as confidential personnel information and shared only with individuals who have a legitimate
business reason to access them.

12.16 Policy Compliance. Managers and employees are responsible for participating in performance reviews according to the applicable schedule and procedures. Exceptions to the
standard review cycle require appropriate management or Human Resources approval.

8.1 Probation Period. All newly hired full-time employees are subject to a standard probationary period of 90 calendar days beginning on their employment start date. The
probationary period is used to evaluate the employee's suitability for the position and does not
automatically result in confirmation.

8.2 Probation Evaluation. During probation, employees are evaluated based on job performance, quality of work, attendance, punctuality, communication, conduct, and ability to
perform the responsibilities associated with their position.

8.3 Initial Evaluation. The employee's manager should conduct an initial performance review after approximately 30 calendar days. The review may identify performance gaps, training
requirements, or other areas requiring improvement before the end of probation.

8.4 Mid-Probation Review. A second evaluation should normally take place around the 60th calendar day of probation. Managers may provide written or verbal feedback regarding progress
toward the expectations of the position.

8.5 Final Probation Evaluation. Before the end of the 90-day probationary period, the manager must evaluate the employee's overall performance and provide a recommendation regarding
confirmation, extension, or termination of employment in accordance with applicable
procedures.

8.6 Confirmation of Employment. An employee who successfully satisfies the applicable performance and conduct requirements may be confirmed as a regular employee after
completion of the probationary period. Confirmation must be documented through the
designated HR process.

8.7 Probation Extension. When additional time is required to evaluate an employee's performance, probation may be extended for up to 30 calendar days with manager and HR
approval. The employee should be informed of the extension before the original probation
period expires.

8.8 Performance Improvement During Probation. When an employee does not meet one or more expected performance standards, the manager may identify specific improvement
requirements and provide appropriate guidance or training. Additional review may be
conducted before a final confirmation decision is made.

8.9 Attendance During Probation. Employees are expected to maintain regular attendance and follow their approved work schedules during probation. Excessive unapproved absence or
repeated lateness may be considered during the probation evaluation.

8.10 Remote Work During Probation. Employees in their probationary period are not automatically eligible for a regular remote or hybrid work arrangement. Remote work during
probation requires manager approval and must comply with the applicable Remote & Hybrid
Work Policy.

8.11 Confirmation Documentation. HR should record the employee's confirmation, probation extension, or other final employment decision in the employee's personnel record. Verbal
statements by coworkers or team members do not constitute formal confirmation.

8.12 Early Confirmation. An employee may be considered for confirmation before completing the full 90-day probationary period when the manager determines that sufficient performance
evidence is available and HR approves the early confirmation.

8.13 Probationary Review Deadline. Managers should submit the final probation evaluation to HR no later than 5 business days before the scheduled end of the probationary period
whenever practicable.

8.14 Policy Compliance. Managers and HR representatives are responsible for following the applicable probation procedures and maintaining appropriate evaluation records. Completion of
the probationary period alone does not constitute confirmation unless the required
confirmation process has been completed.

4.1 Remote Work Eligibility. Full-time employees whose positions are designated as remote- eligible may request a regular remote or hybrid work arrangement after completing 90 calendar
days of employment. Employees in their initial probationary period require specific manager
approval before working remotely.

4.2 Hybrid Work Schedule. Employees approved for the standard hybrid arrangement are expected to work from the office at least 2 days per week and may work remotely for up to 3
days per week. Managers may designate specific in-office days when team coordination requires
common attendance.

4.3 Increased Office Attendance. Certain positions may require employees to work from the office 3 or 4 days per week when their responsibilities require physical collaboration, access to
restricted equipment, supervision, or customer interaction.

4.4 Fully Remote Employees. Employees approved as fully remote are not required to maintain the standard 2-day weekly office schedule. However, they may be required to attend approved
in-person meetings, training sessions, or organizational events.

4.5 Temporary Remote Work. Employees may request temporary remote work for a specific circumstance. Temporary remote work must normally be approved before the employee works
from an alternative location. Temporary remote work lasting more than 10 consecutive business
days requires HR review.

4.6 Remote Work Location. Employees must normally work from their approved remote-work location. Working temporarily from another city or country requires approval when the change
may affect security, working hours, legal requirements, or operational availability.

4.7 Standard Remote Equipment. Employees approved for regular remote work may receive an organization-managed laptop, one monitor, keyboard, mouse, and headset when required by
their role. Equipment provisioning depends on role requirements and available organizational
resources.

4.8 Additional Equipment. Additional monitors, peripherals, or other equipment may be requested when justified by an employee's responsibilities. Additional equipment costing more
than $300 requires manager approval and may require IT or procurement review.

4.9 Equipment Return. Employees must return organization-issued equipment in working condition within 10 business days of their last working day unless IT provides different
instructions.

4.10 Remote Work Approval. Employees requesting a change from office-based work to a regular hybrid or remote arrangement should submit the request at least 10 business days
before the requested effective date. Approval is based on the employee's role, performance,
operational requirements, and team needs.

4.11 Working Hours. Remote and hybrid employees must remain available during their scheduled working hours and must meet the same attendance and performance requirements
that apply when working from the office.

4.12 Policy Exceptions. Exceptions to the standard remote and hybrid work requirements require appropriate management approval and, where specified, HR approval. An exception
granted to one employee does not automatically apply to other employees.

13.1 Training Eligibility. Regular full-time employees who have completed at least 90 calendar days of employment may request company-sponsored training when the training is relevant to
their current responsibilities or an approved development plan.

13.2 Probationary Employees. Employees in their probationary period are not normally eligible for company-sponsored external courses unless the training is required for their position or
specifically approved by their manager and Human Resources.

13.3 Approved Training Courses. Company-sponsored courses must be relevant to the employee's current role, required for compliance, or included in an approved professional
development plan. Training selected solely for personal interest may not qualify for company
sponsorship.

13.4 Manager Approval. Employees must obtain manager approval before registering for a company-sponsored course. The manager should confirm that the training is relevant to the
employee's responsibilities and that the employee's absence from normal duties can be
accommodated.

13.5 Training Budget. Eligible employees may receive company-sponsored training up to $1,000 per calendar year. Amounts above the annual limit require additional approval from the
department head and Human Resources.

13.6 Certification Reimbursement. The company may reimburse eligible employees for professional certification examination fees when the certification is relevant to the employee's
current role or an approved career-development plan. Certification reimbursement is limited to
$750 per certification unless an exception is approved.

13.7 Pre-Approval Requirement. Employees must obtain written approval before registering for a reimbursable certification examination. Payment for an examination made before approval is
not automatically eligible for reimbursement.

13.8 Certification Renewal. Renewal fees for an existing professional certification may be reimbursed when the certification remains relevant to the employee's role. Renewal
reimbursement is subject to the applicable annual training budget and approval requirements.

13.9 Course Completion. Employees receiving company-sponsored training are expected to complete the approved course. When an employee withdraws from a course without an
approved reason, the company may review whether the associated costs remain eligible for
reimbursement.

13.10 Certification Result. Reimbursement of an approved certification examination does not depend on passing the examination unless the applicable certification program or written
approval specifies otherwise. Employees should provide the required examination
documentation after completing the certification process.

13.11 Reimbursement Documentation. Employees requesting reimbursement must submit proof of payment and the required course or examination documentation through the
designated expense process. Reimbursement requests should normally be submitted within 30
calendar days after completion of the course or examination.

13.12 External Training During Working Hours. Employees attending approved training during scheduled working hours must coordinate their absence with their manager. Approval for
training does not automatically modify the employee's regular work schedule.

13.13 Online Training. Approved online courses may qualify for company sponsorship when the course meets the same relevance and approval requirements as other training programs.
Employees must use approved accounts or platforms when company access is provided.

13.14 Required Training. Training required by the company for an employee's position, security responsibilities, safety requirements, or regulatory obligations may be funded outside the
employee's discretionary professional-development budget.

13.15 Employment Changes. Employees who transfer to another department should confirm whether previously approved training remains relevant to their new role. A change in position
does not automatically cancel training that has already been approved and scheduled.

13.16 Policy Compliance. Employees and managers are responsible for following the approval, budget, completion, and reimbursement requirements of this policy. Exceptions to the standard
training or certification limits require appropriate management and Human Resources approval.
